summary: Mexico's economy grew 1.5% in the second quarter, beating forecasts on record exports and World Cup-linked consumption. Fitch estimates the US effective tariff rate on Mexican goods has eased to 3.7%, even as Mexico presses Washington to cut steel tariffs from 50% to the UK's 10% rate ahead of the next US-Mexico-Canada Agreement review. Separately, Pemex and Petrobras are studying deepwater and pre-salt assets in the Gulf of Mexico to reduce exploration risk.

lead.h1: Mexico's economy grows 1.5% in second quarter, beating forecasts
lead.context: Growth was driven by record exports and consumption tied to the World Cup, offering an upside surprise amid ongoing trade tensions with the United States.
lead.background: Mexico's statistics agency reports quarterly economic growth against the prior three-month period, a different measure from the annual figure. Full-year 2025 growth was only about 0.6%, so a single strong quarter needs that pace as context.
lead.view: The 1.5% quarter-on-quarter gain beat forecasts of 1.4%, but exports and World Cup-related spending are one-off drivers rather than proof of a durable shift in the growth rate. Fixed investment fell from 23.8% to 22.4% of gross domestic product in 2025, the number that would need to reverse before a strong export quarter turns into lasting capacity. A record export quarter can coexist with the same weak link between trade and household income that produced 2025's 0.6% growth.
lead.prediction: The most likely path is a slowdown in the third quarter once World Cup consumption fades, unless investment data show new capacity being built rather than existing plants running harder. That would be contradicted by a rise in the investment share of gross domestic product alongside continued export strength.

items.headline: Fitch says the US effective tariff rate on Mexican goods eases to 3.7%
items.context: The rating agency's estimate reflects changes in US trade policy and trade flows, easing concern over the tariff burden on Mexican exports even as broader negotiations continue.
items.background: The United States taxes Mexican exports through overlapping tariff regimes, including duties tied to Section 301 authority and country-specific rates that depend on whether goods meet the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement's regional-content rules.
items.view: An effective tariff rate of 3.7% looks manageable next to blanket duties elsewhere, but the figure blends US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement-compliant goods entering tariff-free with non-compliant goods facing a 10% rate or higher sectoral tariffs, so it masks which exporters are actually exposed. The rate could shift again once the pending Section 301 ruling on manufacturing capacity is decided, since that case sits outside the calculation Fitch used.
items.prediction: The effective tariff rate is likely to stay near this level only until the Section 301 ruling is issued, at which point it could move in either direction depending on the decision. That view would be wrong if the rate changes without any new US tariff action, which would mean trade-flow shifts rather than policy are driving it.

items.headline: Mexico presses Washington to cut steel tariffs to the UK's 10% rate
items.context: Mexico argues its trade surplus position with the United States undercuts the case for the 50% steel tariff, and wants relief before the next review of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement round.
items.background: Section 232 tariffs on steel imports, currently 50% for Mexico, are separate from the Section 301 capacity investigation and from US-Mexico-Canada trade agreement-specific treatment, and the United Kingdom has negotiated a lower 10% rate under the same authority.
items.view: Mexico's ask rests on a data point, a 36.6% drop in steel exports to the United States in 2025, showing the tariff is already cutting trade rather than protecting an oversupply scenario. Whether Washington grants UK-style treatment will depend on the September review round rather than on the trade-surplus argument alone, since the two governments are negotiating multiple tariff tracks at once.
items.prediction: Mexico is likely to keep pressing for a rate cut through the September review round without securing a decision beforehand. That view is wrong if Washington announces a steel tariff adjustment for Mexico ahead of the scheduled round.

items.headline: Pemex and Petrobras study deepwater and pre-salt assets in the Gulf of Mexico
items.context: The state oil companies aim to reduce exploration risk and open new opportunities in Pemex's offshore portfolio through technical cooperation.
items.background: Pemex has struggled with deepwater exploration because it lacks the technical experience Petrobras built in Brazil's pre-salt fields, one of the most complex offshore plays in the world.
items.view: Sharing seismic data and exploration methods is a low-cost way for Pemex to reduce risk on projects it could not otherwise justify funding alone. This is a technical cooperation agreement, not a joint venture or capital commitment, so it does not address Pemex's financing gap or change the money the government spends propping up the company. Any output from these eight offshore assets is years away even under a favorable outcome.
items.prediction: Pemex and Petrobras are likely to spend months to years on data review before any drilling decision follows. That view would be wrong if either company announces a capital commitment or a specific well to be drilled rather than continued study.
